item.title: Box Elder County sheriff charged with automobile homicide for deadly crash
item.description:
A blood sample Box Elder County Sheriff Kevin Potter gave voluntarily two hours after an Oct. 27 Ogden crash measured .065, above Utah's .05 limit, and charges say his level at the time of the crash "was likely higher". Potter has been arrested and charged with second-degree felony automobile homicide in the death of 22-year-old motorcyclist Katie Sue Ruth Huggins, who the charges say had the right-of-way; Ogden Police Capt. Matt Ward, who announced the charges Friday, said Potter failed to yield and that no separate DUI count was filed because the homicide charge already includes it. Potter, who already faces an obstruction charge accusing him of lying about where he was during a separate DUI investigation, remains on paid administrative leave, the county said.

  • Box Elder County sheriff charged with automobile homicide for deadly crash - ksl.com

item.title: Winter weather creates challenges for Utah drivers
item.description:
Utah drivers are crashing more often than at any earlier point this season as snow, rain and cold settle in, and UDOT spokesman Nic Naylor attributed the spike to drivers adjusting, saying "we're not used to this". On Friday, a crash involving a semi closed US-40 for a time and left one person in critical condition, the Utah Highway Patrol said, while canyon regular John Gaspar described the Cottonwood Canyons as "usually a zoo" full of vehicles that should not be heading up there. Naylor said snowplow operators, UDOT's traffic operations center and its meteorologist are coordinating their response, and drivers are urged to slow down, leave extra room and check conditions on the UDOT Traffic website or app.

  • Winter weather creates challenges for Utah drivers - ksl.com

item.title: Spanish Fork community rallies around 25-year-old man injured in hit-and-run
item.description:
Spanish Fork police say a van struck 25-year-old Alan Zelaya as he walked with his brother and mother on Nov. 4 and kept going; investigators later tracked the vehicle down with neighborhood surveillance video, and Maria Del Rocio Morales Ruvalcaba, 51, of Sanpete County now faces a charge of leaving the scene of a crash that caused serious injury; investigators said she told police she thought she had struck a bicycle. Brother Ricky Zelaya, who wrapped his work jacket around Alan's bleeding head, said Alan suffered multiple fractures, among them injuries to his head and pelvis; Alan, who was in a coma after the crash, has since regained consciousness. The Spanish Fork Culver's, where Ricky is a shift manager, is holding a Nov. 30 fundraiser from 5 to 8 p.m., and organizers say all proceeds from food sold that evening will go toward Alan's recovery costs.

item.title: Resorts optimistic about ski season ahead of 2026 Thanksgiving weekend
item.description:
Back-to-back storms have Utah resorts upbeat heading into Thanksgiving week, with Alta spokesperson Lexi Dowdall saying the resort already has a 60-inch base before its planned Wednesday opening, a sharp turn from 2025, when scant early snow pushed Alta's opening back 16 days and the season totaled 321 inches against a typical 550. Ski Utah lists Brighton opening the Tuesday before the holiday and Snowbird and Snowbasin expected on Black Friday, and Ski Utah's Alison Palmintere pointed to the "Super El Niño" pattern as a good sign for snowfall. Dowdall also highlighted a new east wing at Alta's Albion Lodge with 4,000 more square feet of dining space, while reminding skiers that the best part of Alta's season is "in March and April when the snow depth is incredibly deep."

  • Resorts optimistic about ski season ahead of 2026 Thanksgiving weekend - ksl.com

item.title: Woman accused of picking up man, then hitting his wife with SUV
item.description:
Deputies arrested Emery County resident Tabitha Elizabeth Bringhurst, 44, at her home, where they found a black Ford Explorer with marks that appeared to show something sliding down its driver's side, along with the husband of the woman she is accused of hitting. Prosecutors, who have charged her with attempted murder and causing an accident involving serious injury, allege that around 12:30 a.m. Thursday in Orangeville she picked up the man as he walked with his wife, then made a U-turn and struck the wife, who had been arguing with her husband. A neighbor told investigators it was "obvious the driver intended to hit the alleged victim," and the injured woman, bleeding from beneath her chin, went to his home to call 911.

item.title: Nevada man charged in fatal shooting in Granary district
item.description:
Henderson, Nevada, resident Ernesto Rosendo Flores, 24, faces murder and other felony charges filed Friday in the Nov. 7 killing of Evan Cole, 32, in Salt Lake City's Granary district, where, according to charging documents, Cole approached the driver's door of an Audi A5 that had stopped behind his truck before three shots were fired and the car sped off. Detectives say license plate reader searches led them to Flores' Audi and phone records placed his device at the scene, and the charges say he texted his girlfriend that he had to get rid of his phone before he was arrested outside her apartment days later. Calling Flores a flight risk from out of state and citing "the random nature of the incident," prosecutors want him held without bail; the gun allegedly used was still missing as of Friday.

item.title: A reading program tied to the Olympic Games is impacting Utah classrooms
item.description:
Seventy-two Utah elementary schools have adopted Champion Schools 34, a program from Olympic organizers and the Ken Garff for Good initiative that uses reading challenges, an app and athlete videos featuring Olympians and Paralympians to motivate kids eight years ahead of the 2034 Games. Students have logged nearly 7 million reading minutes since September, with some schools reporting participation close to 100%, and Ken Garff for Good president Erin Trenbeath-Murray said adding the Games "just made the excitement exponential". The effort follows a Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute report from early 2026 finding almost half of Utah third graders fall short of grade-level reading expectations, and organizers hope to expand statewide.

item.title: The KSL Vault
item.description:
KSL is launching The KSL Vault, a project sparked by photographer Ray Boone that will post a different archived news story from the thousands of tapes stored in the station's basement to a special YouTube channel each night, giving reports that once aired a single time a second audience. Cabrero writes that the old footage shows a less crowded Utah, with farm fields where southern Salt Lake County suburbs now stand, alongside familiar debates over housing costs, traffic and development, and oddities like a Provo apartment complex that wanted to ban MTV. Retired anchor Keith McCord, who spent 39 years at KSL, introduces the series with Cabrero, and it also resurfaces familiar past faces such as Dick Nourse, Mark Eubank and Jane Clayson.

item.title: Exam shows that hat Fiona the hippo ate was deep into her small intestine
item.description:
The Cincinnati Zoo said Friday that a necropsy found the hat Fiona swallowed had lodged in the middle of her small intestine, 25 feet beyond her final stomach compartment, so far along that no supportive care could have saved the 9-year-old hippo. "No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success," said Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health, who added that surgery was impossible given the hat's location and hippo anatomy. Fans have left flowers and crayon-written notes on a hippo statue at the zoo, and the Field Museum in Chicago confirmed it received the remains of a Cincinnati Zoo hippo that died in 1923 after a boy threw a rubber ball into its mouth.

  • Exam shows that hat Fiona the hippo ate was deep into her small intestine - ksl.com

item.title: Prosecutors abandon plan to use AI simulation of murdered woman's voice in death penalty case
item.description:
Weber County prosecutors told Judge Michael DiReda on Friday that they are dropping their bid to play an AI clone of Joyce Yost's voice at the 2027 re-sentencing of Douglas Lovell, who admitted in 1993 to killing Yost so she could not testify against him in a 1985 rape case, and whose second death sentence the state's high court threw out in 2024. The county had generated the voice with an ElevenLabs tool trained on snippets of a police interview, hoping to present Yost's 1985 preliminary hearing testimony, which survives only as a transcript; after an August hearing where Lovell's defense brought two experts to oppose it, ElevenLabs refused to license its software for the purpose. Chief Criminal Deputy Attorney Branden Miles told the judge the county has been unable to find another provider willing to help; prosecutors have previously had human proxies read Yost's words, and the re-sentencing is scheduled for September 2027.


Sources:

  • Prosecutors abandon plan to use AI simulation of murdered woman's voice in death penalty case - ksl.com

item.title: Hurricane-based nonprofit partners with Indigenous leaders on upcoming Native American exhibit
item.description:
Liberty Village, a 32-acre Hurricane site founded by Lex Howard in 2022 to recreate 18th-century American landmarks as to-scale replicas, is developing a Future Native Village exhibit with Indigenous tribal members, among them Betsy "Red Ant" LaFontaine of the Navajo Nation; no completion date has been set. LaFontaine, who is also involved with the NATIVE endowment, said the aim is to add to history rather than subtract from it, arguing that "America could not have been formed without the Native people." A dedicatory event Saturday, which also marks Native American Heritage Month, is set to feature drumming, dancing, oral history, powwow circles and flute playing by Southern Paiute tribal members.

item.title: UHSAA takes first step toward 2027-29 realignment with debut of Competitive Realignment Index
item.description:
Utah High School Activities Association trustees opened the 2027-29 realignment Thursday by finalizing a new Competitive Realignment Index, keeping general sports at 77% enrollment, 13% socioeconomic data and 10% performance while moving football from a provisional 85-8-7 draft to a 65-13-22 split that more than triples the weight of three years of on-field results. After reviewing index scores with school names hidden, the board set initial class sizes, growing 6A from its current 17 teams to 22 for 11-man football and 21 for general sports. Schools may no longer appeal to drop a class over competitive struggles, only over geography and travel, and the board reconvenes Dec. 1 ahead of final approval Dec. 17, with competition under the new alignment beginning in August 2027.

  • UHSAA takes first step toward 2027-29 realignment with debut of Competitive Realignment Index - ksl.com

item.title: Nasdaq wipes out gains for the year as Anthropic IPO fails to quell AI nerves
item.description:
A worsening tech sell-off erased the Nasdaq's gains for the year Friday with a 5.28% drop, while the S&P 500 fell 3.7% for a seventh straight losing day, its longest such streak since February 2020, and both it and the Dow closed in correction. Anthropic's newly public shares slid 9% to $88.30, just above the $83 IPO price, and Nvidia finished its worst week since October 2008 down 22.7%, as investors weighed returns on AI spending, how newly elected Democratic governors might affect the data center buildout, and Nvidia's role after CEO Jensen Huang resigned. Some strategists think the fears may be overblown: JPMorgan Asset Management's David Kelly likened the slump to "a mild cold" that he expects to pass within a week or two, and CFRA's Arun Sundaram said "the fundamentals don't really justify all this selling".

item.title: Utah man charged with exploiting and enticing teen girl in West Virginia
item.description:
Officers who searched the Pleasant Grove home of Russell Dillon Woodard, 41, on Tuesday seized numerous devices, including one the affidavit says was hidden between his mattress and box spring, and investigators say they are "concerned there are other victims yet to be uncovered". Woodard faces 18 felony charges in 4th District Court, among them 10 first-degree aggravated sexual exploitation counts. A police affidavit alleges he coached a 14-year-old West Virginia girl into producing explicit photos while leading her to believe he was also a minor, though he was about 40 at the time; Pittsburgh FBI agents had alerted local police that one of multiple adult men allegedly abusing the girl online appeared to live in Pleasant Grove.

item.title: Utah picks new water agent as battle over Colorado River continues
item.description:
Gov. Spencer Cox has named Zach Renstrom, general manager of the Washington County Water Conservancy District, as Utah's water agent, a post lawmakers created in 2024 to seek supplies from beyond the state's borders and previously held by Joel Ferry, who left as natural resources commissioner in August. Senate President Stuart Adams, who sponsored the bill creating the role, backed the choice, crediting Renstrom with a "practical understanding" of turning big water plans into finished projects. The appointment follows the Colorado River Basin states' failure to agree on managing Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which led to a federal 10-year plan that Nevada and Arizona have sued over because of mandatory cuts for Lower Basin states.

item.title: Fiona's death gives parents a chance to teach kids about grief — and life
item.description:
For many children, the death of Fiona, the 9-year-old Cincinnati Zoo hippo who died Thursday after swallowing a knit hat, may be their first loss of an animal they loved, and psychologists and grief specialists say it can give parents an opening to talk about death. Experts advise plain, age-appropriate explanations that Fiona is not coming back, warning that euphemisms such as "went to sleep" can confuse or scare young kids, and say parents can share their own sadness and return to the subject over time. Samantha Haines of St. Petersburg, Florida, said she and her hippo-loving 10-year-old cried together for about 20 minutes, while a Wisconsin mother said her 8-year-old took comfort in picturing Fiona in heaven with the family dog.

  • Fiona's death gives parents a chance to teach kids about grief — and life - ksl.com

item.title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
item.description:
As Thanksgiving travel week gets underway, some fliers are uneasy after last week's rare nationwide ground stop, the longest since 9/11, a separate airline outage and a string of other tech failures, though UNLV aviation historian Dan Bubb said grumbling travelers "are still going to do it." The bigger pain may be price: Hopper estimated in late October that roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas are up 39% and 40% from a year ago, the highest holiday fares in a decade, with some increases tied to jet fuel costs linked to the war in Iran. Miami frequent flier Michelle Jolene, who says delays no longer rattle her, covered her daughter's flight home from Washington, D.C., with roughly 8,500 American Airlines miles earned by buying 10 boxes of toilet paper through the airline's shopping portal.

item.title: UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging to rebuild ties after Brexit
item.description:
At a Brussels summit Friday, Britain and the EU sealed agreements that drop checks on farm and food trade, connect the two emissions trading systems and open up to three years of residence and work for 100,000 young adults in each direction, while giving themselves six months to settle tuition fees for each other's students. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has said rejoining the bloc should remain an option though it is far from imminent, called the package a "historic moment" and estimated it could add 0.5% to Britain's economy. Brexit supporters object that Britain must accept EU rules it has no hand in setting, and Nigel Farage, who leads Reform UK, told the BBC the Brexit debate "has just started again".

item.title: European troops from 11 countries hold a drill in Poland for a potential postwar Ukraine mission
item.description:
About 2,800 personnel from nine European countries, with Poland handling logistics and Turkey taking part remotely from Istanbul, are in a two-week exercise at Poland's Nowa Deba training ground that for the first time tests whether the France- and U.K.-led Coalition of the Willing could deploy to Ukraine after the war. If sent once a ceasefire holds, the force would help rebuild Ukraine's military, provide the reassurance needed to reopen its airspace and clear Black Sea mines, its commander has said, though it would have no peacekeeping role, and U.K. Brig. Campbell Close said, "We are a defensive force." The drill overlapped with a Russian missile crash about 47 miles away that Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called likely an intentional provocation, and Putin warned last year that any foreign troops in Ukraine would be "legitimate targets."

  • European troops from 11 countries hold a drill in Poland for a potential postwar Ukraine mission - ksl.com

item.title: UN climate talks slammed by activists, leaders as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft agreement
item.description:
The draft final agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, never mentions fossil fuels, setting off an uproar among activists and national leaders on Friday, the last scheduled day, though negotiators expect talks to spill into Saturday. Its main electrification goal, lifting electricity's share of global energy use from about 21% to 35% by 2035, doesn't specify renewable power, and a fund for climate-ravaged nations would be tripled with no dollar amount, while summit overseer Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, argued the electrification push implies a move away from fossil fuels. Panama threatened to "formally object" absent changes such as an oil production cap, and its environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, called the summits "an exercise in hypocrisy and futility".


Sources:

  • UN climate talks slammed by activists, leaders as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft agreement - ksl.com

item.title: Poland says a Russian missile that crashed in its territory was a provocation
item.description:
A Russian Kh-101 missile came down in Poland about 37 miles from the Ukrainian border Friday, apparently in a wooded area and with no immediate reports of injuries or damage, during an overnight Russian barrage of 400-plus drones and more than 110 missiles that Zelenskyy said killed at least eight civilians in Ukraine. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the crash appeared to be "an intentional provocation" timed to European military exercises under way in Poland, and NATO chief Mark Rutte called it a "grave violation" of Polish airspace. The strikes came hours after Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian attacks on a bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia, and a Ukrainian deputy energy minister said hits on the power grid forced the country's three operating nuclear plants to cut output.

item.title: Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail
item.description:
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday laid out a plan to shut the Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, well past a 2027 legal deadline the city is all but certain to miss, by cutting the number of people held there from more than 6,500 to around 4,500. The approach relies on new diversion and supervised release programs, expanded housing and social services, a restored online bail payment option and fewer case delays, with people shifted to borough jails expected to open from 2029 in Brooklyn through 2032 in Manhattan. Violence and overcrowding at Rikers had prompted a federal judge to appoint an outside manager, and in announcing the plan Mamdani said, "It is time to finally close Rikers Island".

item.title: Woman who survived hundreds-foot fall on Mount Timpanogos credits rescuers for saving her life
item.description:
Utah schoolteacher Amber Baumgartner is recovering from a broken neck, a broken elbow and other injuries after slipping on Oct. 26 while descending Mount Timpanogos and sliding hundreds of feet down a snowy slope to a small ledge, where she held herself in place for over an hour. With 911 calls dropping, her hiking group reached Utah County Sheriff's Office Search and Rescue by text, and its airplane pilot spotted her and coordinated with a Utah Department of Public Safety helicopter crew to reach her. Friend Josh Dunn said that when she asked a rescuer whether she would fall, he answered something like "No, I've got you," and friends have started a GoFundMe for her medical costs.

item.title: 'These kids deserve better': Mother speaks out after son's unlawful school seclusions
item.description:
A mother identified only as Lori told the KSL Investigators that her autistic 6-year-old son, Gunner, was secluded twice in kindergarten at the Davis School District's Orchard Elementary months after a 2025 law banned the practice for kindergartners, and that he has since grown scared of school and been secluded several more times in first grade. The district declined an interview, citing federal student privacy law and saying seclusion is a last resort, while state data show 1,565 seclusion incidents in 2025-26, up 37%, a rise state board coordinator Krisanne Lewis said is hard to read given increased scrutiny and policy and definition changes. Nate Crippes of the Disability Law Center said "Clearly our system is not working," and 15 state compliance letters obtained by KSL describe untrained staff, seclusions past the 30-minute limit and another secluded kindergartner.

item.title: Lehi family pays it forward after contractors donate garage remodel in son's memory
item.description:
After 20-year-old Dominic Millward, who loved fixing cars, died last month after drinking an unknown substance, JD Hepworth of Nova Concrete Coatings showed up at the family's Lehi home to bid an epoxy garage floor his mother had forgotten requesting, then rallied The Coating House, other suppliers and contractors, and sign company Notatek to remodel the garage in his memory for free. Mary Millward said sorting her son's tools with his friends was "very healing" and that she and her husband are putting memorial funds toward the medical debt of a young mother who had posted online looking for odd jobs and came to help clear the space. She said her next step is to keep helping others and "just keep doing good."

item.title: Salt Lake County 'Giving Tree' brings hope to older adults this holiday season
item.description:
Many tags on Salt Lake County Aging and Adult Services' Giving Tree, where donors pick an older adult's first name, age and wish list, are asking for basics this year, such as grocery and gas gift cards, blankets and walking sneakers. The agency's Emma Furman tied that to high gas and grocery prices, noting that Meals on Wheels, which supplied most recipients, has seen enrollment rise 28% this year, and said the goal is to fulfill wishes for 300 seniors. Gifts are due Nov. 30 at the county government center for volunteers to deliver in December, and Lea Robledo of the Liberty Senior Center said a warm meal for isolated seniors "changes their whole day."

item.title: Utah drivers can check canyon traction-law readiness with new UDOT quiz
item.description:
With snow piling up in the Wasatch Mountains, UDOT spokesperson Nic Naylor is urging Cottonwood Canyons visitors to take the agency's online traction law quiz, which helps drivers confirm their tires carry the M+S or three-peak mountain snowflake marking and have at least 5/32 of an inch of tread. Drivers can have their tread checked for free at locations listed on UDOT's website and get this year's new sticker, which Naylor said lets enforcers see a car's tires have been checked so it can "get up the canyon a little faster." Naylor said drivers should "prepare for and plan before you even hit the road," and warned that even rain raises the risk of hydroplaning.

item.title: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
item.description:
The Senate voted 62-33 Thursday to pass a bipartisan overhaul meant to speed permitting for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects and make data centers pay for the energy they use, sending it to the House, which passed a narrower, industry-friendly version last year. Negotiated by Republicans Shelley Moore Capito and Utah's Mike Lee with Democrats Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, the bill drew 15 Democratic votes plus backing from Trump and industry groups, and Lee said it would make it "easier to build in America again". Environmental groups, tribal leaders and Democrats including Jeff Merkley and Maria Cantwell objected to limits on judicial review and changes to laws such as NEPA, with Jen Duggan of the Environmental Integrity Project calling it "a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America".

item.title: USU researchers highlight Great Salt Lake concerns, improving air quality in report to lawmakers
item.description:
Utah State University's Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water and Air delivered its annual report to the governor and Legislature, adding a new section on how lawmakers can handle data centers' demands on water and energy, while flagging the Great Salt Lake and noting that air quality keeps improving despite growth in population and power production. Institute executive director Anna McEntire said a lack of spring snow made 2026 "a rough year" of drought, wildfire and strain on farmers, and urged more precise use of water if winter stays dry. Newly elected state Rep. Patrick Belmont, a USU professor, said the lake "is worse off now than it was seven years ago" and that lawmakers should check whether spending is actually getting water to it.

item.title: Get Gephardt helps Salt Lake woman fight a hotel no-show charge
item.description:
Michelle Hill was hit with a $224 no-show penalty for a third room she had reserved through Booking.com at St. George's Coronada Inn & Suites over Easter weekend, even though the hotel couldn't find that reservation when her family arrived and she spent the stay in the other two rooms. Hill said the hotel first agreed she was owed a refund but later claimed she had initiated the cancellation; after Get Gephardt reached out, Booking.com did not respond, but an attorney for the hotel said "upper management agreed" she should get a full refund and asked the hotel to send her a check directly, and Hill got her money back. The KSL Investigators note that booking through a third-party travel site can save money but complicates matters when something goes wrong.

item.title: Florida conducts record 20th execution of 2026 on same day Texas set to put a man to death
item.description:
Florida executed Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, on Thursday for the 1991 strangling of Michael and Susan MacIvor and the death of their unborn child in the Florida Keys, its 20th execution of 2026, a state record that tops the 19 carried out in 2025 under Gov. Ron DeSantis. Overton, linked to the crime by a DNA sample taken after an unrelated 1996 burglary arrest, maintained his innocence to the end, saying "I never killed anyone." Texas was set to execute Reinaldo Dennes, 70, about an hour later for the 1996 killing of Houston diamond dealer Janos Szucs during a $3.6-million heist, a pairing that spotlights the aging of the U.S. death row population.

item.title: Livestock association highlights $10,000 reward after lamb killed on Cedar Mountain
item.description:
A 7-month-old lamb owned by James Davis of LX Livestock was shot and left on Kolob Road on Cedar Mountain between Nov. 14 and 15, prompting the Cedar Livestock Association to call attention again to its $10,000 reward for information. Association President Sandy Webster said the reward, posted on signs for about 15 years after a string of sheep and cattle were shot and abandoned along the road, has not drawn a single lead, and the Iron County Sheriff's Office asks anyone with information to call Detective McIntyre at 435-867-7500. Davis, who has ranched on the mountain since the 1980s, said the lamb was found "right near a reward sign for information on shooting sheep."

item.title: Utah family, friends and strangers search for missing Marine in California
item.description:
Marriner Richards, a 19-year-old Marine from Syracuse, Utah, stationed at the Twentynine Palms Marine Corps base, has been missing since walking out of the Tortoise Rock Casino in Twentynine Palms, California, on Nov. 7, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Office. Jenny Smith of the sheriff's office said deputies and detectives have canvassed nearby residents and businesses and searched neighboring Joshua Tree National Park with off-road vehicles and aircraft. His father, Brock Richards, said more than 40 locals turned out to search one day and 20 the next, and members of the family's church congregation and neighborhood were driving down from Utah to join more searches.

item.title: Sen. Curtis: Pay Utah's federal workers legit wages — or wave bye-bye to talent
item.description:
Utah Sen. John Curtis on Thursday introduced the Locality Pay Fairness and Improvement Act, which would rework how federal locality pay is calculated to weigh local housing costs, blue-collar wages and labor market conditions, after hearing concerns from federal workers at places like Hill Air Force Base that most Utah employees get the same adjustment as those in cheaper labor markets. The bill calls for an independent study, a multi-year research program and a pilot program, with Curtis saying Utah stakeholders are "anxious to be part of that pilot program" and warning that if federal workers "can't afford that house payment, we can't keep them." A similar amendment to the defense authorization bill failed last year after the American Federation of Government Employees opposed it, reportedly over fears the Trump administration would use it to cut pay, though Curtis said a union executive has since apologized.

item.title: Former Salt Lake rec center becomes affordable housing
item.description:
One-bedroom apartments start at $999 a month, with lower rents for income-qualifying households, at Innovation Park at Liberty Wells, a 66-home Salt Lake City development of townhomes and apartments that opened Thursday inside a converted neighborhood recreation center at 707 S. 400 East. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints donated the land, Ivory Innovations and the Call to Action Foundation partnered on the project, and Elder John A. McCune said people who once gathered there for recreation will now "call it their homes". Ivory Innovations founder Clark Ivory said visitors are amazed by what became of the old gym, and Mayor Erin Mendenhall said the units are affordable even for households earning well below the average family.

item.title: Trump administration moves to have lawsuit dismissed in challenge to Alaska's US Senate race
item.description:
The Justice Department on Thursday asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to declare moot its suit, filed at President Donald Trump's direction, to block certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's win in Alaska's U.S. Senate race over a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot, while also asking the court to vacate the lower court's dismissal. Peltola won an outright majority, Democrats' ninth Senate pickup, and the margin exceeded the votes cast for the second Sullivan, a retired Petersburg schoolteacher whom documents reported by The New York Times appeared to tie to recruiting by Peltola's campaign, which both deny. Alaska's Republican-led state government had called the administration's move legally "meritless"; it is the second high-profile election case the department has moved to drop since Nov. 3, after one targeting roughly 20,000 California ballots.

item.title: Hooper man faces 41 felony counts, including 21 for secretly recording children
item.description:
Jeremy Jack Hall, 44, of Hooper faces 41 felony counts filed Monday by Weber County prosecutors, the most serious being an aggravated sexual exploitation charge alleging that in 2024 he made abuse material depicting a young girl, apparently in a church classroom. Charging documents say Roy police, acting on a tip, found sexually explicit videos of children plus 27 more recordings of young girls in a cloud account, and that Hall, who appeared to serve as a teacher or youth leader for children ages 8 to 10, "admitted to secretly recording the juveniles" while acting as their teacher. The remaining charges are 19 exploitation counts for possessing abuse material and 21 voyeurism counts tied mostly to late 2025 and 2026; Hall is jailed ahead of a Dec. 3 court date.

item.title: Kim Ziebarth named Tooele Technical College president
item.description:
Kim Ziebarth, a former interim president and vice president at Davis Technical College, will take over as president of Tooele Technical College on Jan. 1, 2027, after the state board of education voted unanimously Thursday to appoint her. Ziebarth has also been the Utah System of Higher Education's associate commissioner for technical education and a senior adviser to Commissioner Geoffrey Landward, and has held national roles with the Council on Occupational Education and the National Technical Honor Society. Ziebarth said Tooele County "has tremendous opportunity ahead," and Landward cited her "genuine commitment to students and to the future of technical education" in a statement.

item.title: Prosecutors call Tyler Robinson request for materials used in UVU report a 'fishing expedition'
item.description:
The Utah County Attorney's Office told 4th District Court on Thursday that it will not turn over most of the materials Tyler Robinson's defense requested from the independent After-Action Report that UVU commissioned after Charlie Kirk's killing, arguing that the project team behind the report has "no tie to the prosecution" and that the materials aren't in its possession or control. The defense's Oct. 6 requests sought items such as the team's interviews, its outreach to Turning Point USA and UVU police rosters for Sept. 10 and 11, 2025, but prosecutors call the request "nothing more than a fishing expedition" because those items served a separate purpose and the investigative files have already been disclosed. UVU has also declined to provide most of the material, though prosecutors noted it has indicated it will share some with defense attorneys; Robinson, charged with aggravated murder and facing a possible death sentence, is set for trial in June 2028.

item.title: The world is experiencing 'GTA VI' together — players and spectators alike
item.description:
Thursday's global launch of Grand Theft Auto VI turned a mostly solitary game into a shared event, with people spending more than 132 million hours watching streams across Twitch, YouTube and Kick on release day and nearly 8 million watching at once at one point, according to Streams Charts. The game has already made an estimated $1.8 billion; Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, citing its 99 out of 100 Metacritic score, called it "a massive creative achievement" for Rockstar, and everyone from the Miami Heat to Uber Eats to the Interior Department joined in the hype. Not everyone cheered: Fox News commentator Kayleigh McEnany said, "I do worry about this effect on a young generation," while some online MAGA voices complained the game isn't as depraved as earlier entries.

item.title: Aerial reseeding operations taking place on Cottonwood Fire burn scar
item.description:
State wildlife and forestry agencies and contractor Hammond Helicopter are flying close to 500 airplane loads of seed out of the Junction airport to reseed about 56,000 acres of the roughly 97,000-acre Cottonwood Fire burn scar between Beaver and Piute counties with some 600,000 pounds of grasses, forbs and shrubs. Bare, burned slopes have already sent mud and debris into communities below and across U.S. 89 and I-15, and the new growth is meant to anchor soil while feeding deer and elk; "The faster we can get roots in the soil to hold that soil up on the mountain, the better," said the Division of Wildlife Resources' Gary Bezzant. The seed will sit dormant in the snow until melt carries it into the soil, and while success hinges on precipitation, forester Nicholas Dastrup said "great soil moisture right now" has crews hopeful.

item.title: 13 men charged in train-heist ring that netted $22M in cargo from major retailers
item.description:
A federal indictment unsealed Thursday in Los Angeles charges 13 men with conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo, alleging they stole more than $22 million in goods such as Nike sneakers, Crocs and power tools from more than three dozen trains carrying imports from the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The indictment alleges the group disabled trains at planned spots by busting the brakes, moved the merchandise onto trucks and sold it to an unnamed company for resale, while the men posted photos of themselves with cash and stolen goods in group chats. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli called the scale of the theft "staggering"; two of the men also face charges of violence against railroad carriers, and convictions could bring five to 20 years in federal prison.

item.title: Anthropic surges in market debut after biggest IPO on record, despite fears that AI is running amok
item.description:
Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, closed up 17% at $97.17 in its first day of trading Thursday after an IPO that overtook SpaceX as the largest ever, at one point topping $2 trillion in value despite worries about an AI bubble, the recent ouster of Nvidia's CEO and a possible crackdown next year by a Democratic-led Congress. The sale of 980 million shares raised $81 billion, and a planned $26 billion private sale was set to bring the total to $107 billion, giving the company, which carries $6.2 billion in debt, is unprofitable under standard accounting rules and has committed to $900 billion in computing and infrastructure spending, room to expand without borrowing more. CEO Dario Amodei pitched the company as proof that it's possible to make "the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company," while analyst Dan Ives called the debut "a big win for the tech sector".

item.title: How renowned artist plans to bring 'love' to Salt Lake City's Fleet Block
item.description:
Salt Lake City Arts Council officials said Thursday that New York artist Kenseth Armstead, chosen from 175 applicants, will create 2 Gather, a 20-foot-tall, 56-foot-wide polished aluminum sculpture spelling the word love in English, Spanish, Shoshoni, Nahuatl and Twi for the former city vehicle fleet parcel known as the Fleet Block. The council wanted a piece that carried the social justice spirit of the 29 murals of people killed by police that covered the site's walls until redevelopment began last year, and Gina Thayne, whose nephew was among those honored, wrote that "our murals were all about love, in so many different languages" in response to Armstead's video about the design. Armstead said of the project's call for artists that they were "asking for care," and the sculpture is expected to be installed by late 2028 or early 2029 in an open space funded with $6 million from the 2022 parks bond and $2 million from a Bezos Earth Fund grant.

item.title: St. George cancer center expansion brings specialized care closer to home
item.description:
Intermountain Health expanded the cancer center at St. George Regional Hospital in September, adding room for more infusion treatments, expanded palliative care and closer teamwork between specialists and support staff, and it has added a neuro-oncologist while recruiting more specialists. Oncologist Dr. Derrick Haslem said some specialized treatments may still require travel to larger hospitals, but consultations, preparation and follow-up can be handled locally, and patients kept close to home will be "so much better off physically, mentally and emotionally". For Pine Valley's Dana Rowley, whose multiple myeloma care has mostly been in St. George but required a trip to Salt Lake City for a stem cell transplant, the expansion hasn't changed his treatment yet, though his wife, Glenda, hopes it will spare other families from traveling as far.

item.title: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo has died, days after ingesting a visitor's hat
item.description:
Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo hippo who became a worldwide sensation after surviving a premature birth in 2017, died Thursday of complications from swallowing a knit hat that a ceiling fan caught and flung into her enclosure after a visitor tossed it in the air about 11 days earlier. Specialists told the zoo surgery wasn't an option for a full-grown hippo, so the care team kept her hydrated, sedated her twice for exams and even borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm in hopes the shaking would move the hat along, but the zoo said it was "ultimately too much to overcome". Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval called Fiona "a symbol of perseverance and joy in Cincinnati"; zoos have warned for years about objects tossed or blown into animal habitats.

item.title: Church History Museum opens three new exhibits to support Salt Lake Temple Celebration
item.description:
Ahead of the Salt Lake Temple Celebration that begins in April 2027, the Church History Museum on Temple Square has opened three exhibits, running until October 2027, on the temple's construction and renovation, depictions of it from around the world, and 55 conversion stories. Artifacts from the April 1893 dedication include the original Tabernacle Choir music stand, a cornet and dedication tickets, and visitors can also see a replica of the Angel Moroni statue, sketch the facade at a drafting table like carpenter-turned-architect Truman Angell, and view 16 first editions of the Book of Mormon in their languages. Museum director Riley Lorimer said the hope is that visitors see the temple as "a living, working building" and come away feeling "the love of God".

item.title: South Korea's top court overturns charges against ex-prime minister for his role in martial law
item.description:
South Korea's Supreme Court voted 9-3 Thursday to overturn former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo's conviction for helping ousted President Yoon Suk Yeol legitimize his December 2024 martial law decree, finding prosecutors hadn't proven Han's intent or that he knew of the plan in advance, and sent the case back to the Seoul High Court, which had imposed a 15-year sentence. The court left standing findings that Han discussed cutting off water and electricity to critical media outlets, falsified and destroyed the proclamation and lied under oath, and Han remains in detention for now. The ruling Democratic Party accused Chief Justice Jo Hee-de of a "judicial insurrection" as the same court separately upheld a four-year prison term on corruption charges for Yoon's wife, Kim Keon Hee.

item.title: Report shows some improvements, red flags in 7 of Utah's major cities
item.description:
The first Annual Data Summaries from the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute and the Cities Strong Foundation found that crime fell between 2021 and 2025 in all seven cities studied (Layton, Ogden, Orem, Provo, Salt Lake City, Santaquin and West Valley City), and that homeowners in five of them are staying in their homes longer. The red flags centered on children and housing: six of the cities had more than a quarter of K-12 students chronically absent in 2024-25, above the 23.8% statewide rate, all seven fall short of Utah's 2030 goal of 80% third-grade reading proficiency, and about half of renters are cost-burdened, spending at least 30% of income on housing. Gardner analyst Heidi Prior said longer-tenured residents are "more likely to build social ties," and the institute plans to update the summaries annually.

item.title: Denmark approves security deal with US and Greenland, seeking to ease tensions
item.description:
Denmark's parliament voted 109-0 Thursday to approve a security deal with the United States and Greenland that paves the way for more U.S. bases on the island, a final step meant to ease months of tension over the Trump administration's pressure for a possible U.S. takeover. Signed in New York in September and building on a 1951 defense agreement, the deal lets the U.S. expand activity at Pituffik Space Base and set up defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, keeps the island under Danish control and would still apply if Greenland becomes independent, and allows only NATO members to establish military installations there. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen wrote that "It hasn't been an easy process" while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the deal "will make us all safer, stronger, and more secure."

item.title: For the first time, UN's highest court finds a country responsible for genocide: Myanmar
item.description:
The International Court of Justice ruled 9-6 on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in its 2017 military campaign in Rakhine state, rejecting Myanmar's claim that it was fighting insurgents and marking the first time the U.N.'s top court has found a country responsible for genocide. The court found Myanmar's forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya and ordered the country to allow the "safe, voluntary and dignified return" of those who fled, prosecute perpetrators and pay compensation in an amount to be set later, though it can only report noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council. The case, brought by Gambia in 2019, drew tearful celebration from Rohingya in The Hague, and Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow said "The victory belongs to the Rohingya."

item.title: Lagoon's new roller coaster honors retired ride while shooting for the stars
item.description:
Lagoon's J3 Grand Prix, due in July 2027 and described by special events director Julie Freed as the first hot racer coaster in the U.S., will be the Farmington park's first multi-launch coaster and its first built by Intamin. Riders at least 4 feet tall will sit alone in cockpits on a 10-seat single-file train and get two launches, three inversions and 12 airtime moments, a change from the retired Jet Star 2, to which the train pays tribute. Freed, who showed off the train Tuesday at the IAAPA Expo in Orlando, said replacing Jet Star 2 reflects the park's aim of "honoring the past" while still seeking "to break records" and innovate.

item.title: International competition to help Salt Lake City as it eyes $58M Civic Center overhaul
item.description:
Salt Lake City will host the 2027 Land Art Generator Initiative competition, which will ask designers worldwide to create a shade structure for the Civic Center that also produces clean electricity, a boost for Mayor Erin Mendenhall's $58 million plan to turn the crumbling, mostly empty plaza between the main library and City Hall into a downtown park (the plan's cost estimate excludes the contest). The plan would trade most of the pavers for water-efficient grass, could add hundreds of trees plus a skate park, playground and dog park, and would yield over 7 net acres of added green space able to hold over 36,000 people at once, with construction possibly starting by the end of 2027 and completion targeted around 2031. Entries are due April 12 and three finalists will each get $50,000; Mendenhall called the selection "very special", and the city hopes the result becomes a revered artwork in the spirit of an urban Spiral Jetty.

item.title: University of Utah snow courses help recreationists prepare for winter
item.description:
University of Utah Continuing Education runs three-day avalanche courses, built to American Avalanche Association standards, that teach students and community members how terrain, weather and snowpack combine and how to use Utah Avalanche Center forecasts to judge risk. Nate Furman, a professor who teaches some of the classes, said instructors stop along the route to teach rescue skills like using an avalanche beacon, and that every few years a former student writes to say the training led to "better decisions" during a real incident. The university also has an online avalanche awareness course and classes ranging from snowboarding to winter backpacking, and Furman said it serves about 1,500 students a year across 60 to 70 outdoor courses.

item.title: Judge issues 14-day extension of order blocking Trump's memorial arch in DC
item.description:
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Wednesday added 14 days to the order she issued Nov. 5 halting construction of President Donald Trump's planned 250-foot arch at Memorial Circle, after the National Capital Planning Commission had approved it 8-4, so work stays paused until Dec. 3 or a ruling on a preliminary injunction. The suits, brought by Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian, the District of Columbia and Virginia, Kennedy family members and Arlington County, argue in part that Congress must approve the arch and that it would spoil sightlines between landmarks, while the administration says Congress cleared the way for a monument there decades ago. White House spokesman Davis Ingle blamed an "activist district court" and said the administration expects to be "fully vindicated" as the case goes on.

item.title: Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians by 2035 as the world's largest religion
item.description:
Muslims are expected to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, 2.57 billion to 2.52 billion, making Islam the largest religion, according to Pew Research Center projections that also have the U.S. losing its Christian majority by 2065. "It's the babies," Pew demographer Conrad Hackett said, explaining that birth rates matter far more than conversion; Pew put the 2020-2025 fertility rate at 3.1 children per Muslim woman against 2.5 for Christians. Alan Cooperman, Pew's director of religion research, warned against portraying the shift as a clash, saying he doesn't think Muslim growth is "coming at the expense of Christians".

item.title: Logan man nearing end of Utah golf bucket list he started with his father
item.description:
Cache Valley golfer Nick Purintun is down to two courses, Marcella in Park City and the exclusive Wasatch Peaks Ranch in Morgan County, in a quest to play every course in Utah that he began as a shared goal with his father. The pair were 10 courses short when Purintun's father fell ill in 2018, and Purintun put his clubs away for a couple of years after the death until his own son pushed him to finish. Purintun, who called the effort "a great journey" and is already toying with a course in all 50 states next, said his father "would be so proud."

item.title: Tooele County Council member, assistant fire chief charged with sex abuse
item.description:
Tooele County Councilman Erik Stromberg, 49, who is also Grantsville's first assistant fire chief, faces three third-degree felony counts of forcible sexual abuse, and the city placed him on administrative leave after KSL reported the charges. Charging documents allege he inappropriately touched his accuser about a dozen times from January to August 2023 and say he told Utah Attorney General's Office agents this month that he had intended to harm the victim emotionally. The attorney general's office took the case, first reported to Grantsville police in 2024, because of a conflict, while the County Council said it "takes allegations of this nature very seriously."

item.title: $500 car deposit receipt leaves refund terms unclear at Utah dealership
item.description:
Bountiful resident Barry McCann paid an Orem dealership $500 to hold a rebuilt-title Honda Pilot for his son, but after an inspection, McCann said, they were advised against buying it, and Avanesyan Motors refused to return the money. McCann insists he was promised a refundable deposit, while managers told KSL the salesperson had explained it was nonrefundable without a mechanic's written report of a significant problem, and the receipt itself shows only the date, the amount and the word "Deposit." The Utah Division of Consumer Protection said businesses must refund deposits unless the policy is "clearly and conspicuously disclosed", and spokesperson Melanie Hall said verbal explanations likely wouldn't meet that bar; McCann plans to file a complaint.

item.title: New 'Toxic Hall of Shame' includes Publix, Trader Joe's and McDonald's
item.description:
Toxic-Free Future's latest retailer report card, shared first with CNN, put 16 major retailers including Trader Joe's, Publix, McDonald's, Wayfair and Williams-Sonoma in its Toxic Hall of Shame with F grades for failing to cut hazardous chemicals and plastics, while Apple got an A, with A- grades for Ikea, Target and Sephora. The average grade was a D+, only 10% of retailers reported measurable reduction goals compared with 44% in 2024, and Walmart and Whole Foods posted the steepest declines to land at C, though Whole Foods said an internal error kept some of its information from reaching the group by the deadline. McDonald's sent CNN a report showing it had reached over 99% of its 2025 target for cutting added fluorinated compounds, but Toxic-Free Future's Mike Schade noted it set no new goals for other problem chemicals and called PFAS "just the tip of the toxic iceberg".

item.title: Vincent van Gogh painting sells for $190 million, smashing auction record
item.description:
Van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs, which shows a burst of chestnut trees at Auvers-sur-Oise from his final months, sold for more than $190 million at Sotheby's in New York on Wednesday after a three-minute bidding contest, far above his previous auction record of $117.2 million. The sale came days after heirs of Samuel Fischer, a Jewish publisher in 1930s Berlin, said the work had been sold under Nazi-era financial pressure; Sotheby's said its provenance research did not support that but announced Tuesday it had reached an agreement with them on undisclosed terms. The 12 works from the Blaquier-Arrieta family's rarely seen collection, which Sotheby's Helena Newman called "a mini Musée d'Orsay" and which the family never lent to museums, brought in almost $412 million, including over $111 million for Cézanne's Arlequin.

item.title: Park City Council votes to table long-discussed housing project
item.description:
After roughly a decade of discussion, the Park City Council voted 3-2 against a Brinshore Development mixed-use project for the Bonanza Park area that would have brought around 90 affordable housing units along with a cafe, retail and outdoor space, and a parking structure. Residents had objected to added traffic and the building's proposed height, and were also upset that the Kimball Arts Center decided in 2025 not to move near the site. Councilwoman Molly Miller lamented the lack of support for affordable housing, warning that service workers will suffer if it keeps disappearing, while Councilman Ed Parigian, objecting that people can sign a piece of paper and think they're on the council, called it "a crazy way to run a town".

item.title: Expert: FBI FLASH advisory highlights AI developments in cyber threats
item.description:
An FBI FLASH advisory posted by the agency's Dallas office warns that state actors and cybercriminals have used ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, to automate attacks, saying it can get from initial targeting to privileged access "in under three hours". Adam Marre, chief information security officer at Arctic Wolf, said the tool was built for defenders who probe organizations for weaknesses, and that while its developer has pulled it, copies of the open-source software remain in circulation. Marre said attackers are finding vulnerabilities at a scale far beyond prior years and urged companies to pair basics like password managers and phishing awareness with stronger defenses, possibly AI-based ones, adding, "Now everybody has to take cybersecurity seriously."

item.title: Utah lawmakers unveil draft legislation aimed at regulating police use of surveillance technology
item.description:
A draft bill presented Wednesday to the Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice Interim Committee would require police agencies to publicly post policies for technology such as automatic license plate readers, run quarterly internal audits and discipline employees who misuse the systems. It leaves out the two safeguards privacy advocates have pressed hardest for, independent audits and a warrant requirement for non-emergency searches; Sen. Calvin Musselman said separate bills would handle specific policies, and Libertas Institute privacy analyst Emily Grimmius said "external audits are much needed for public trust". The proposal comes a week after a KSL Investigation found a former Tooele County detective had used the department's plate-reader system to look up the vehicle of the estranged husband of a woman the detective was seeing, misconduct that a routine audit did not uncover.

item.title: Promise that started at age 11 grows into Thanksgiving meals for 3,600 Utah families
item.description:
Thanksgiving Heroes, which grew out of a promise founder Rob Adams made to his mother at age 11 after others helped his struggling family, is expected to provide Thanksgiving meals to 3,600 Utah families through a Saturday distribution at a Draper warehouse. Golf tournaments, concerts and other events pay for the groceries, and Adams said planning that once began around Halloween now starts at the beginning of the year. Donations are behind this year as food prices climb and the need grows, Adams said, though "every year the miracle shows up."

item.description:
Ahead of the Salt Lake Temple's six-month open house starting next April, the Church History Museum on Temple Square has opened three exhibits, including artifacts from the temple's April 1893 dedication such as the original Tabernacle Choir music stand, dedication tickets and attendees' journal entries. One by One gathers 55 personal faith stories from 40 countries, Fitly Framed Together traces the craftsmen and members who built the temple, and All Nations Shall Flow Into It displays art from around the world. Curator Emily Utt said the public got about two hours inside before the 1893 dedication, with a couple hundred people admitted, and added, "We want the world to come and be with us."

item.title: The etiquette you're not thinking about: Healthy ways to talk about food this holiday season
item.description:
KSL health contributor Miki Eberhardt says holiday etiquette should extend beyond table manners to how families talk about food and bodies. Weight changes can stem from grief, anxiety, illness or disordered eating, so a weight-loss compliment can land badly; "You could be praising someone's really hard thing," Eberhardt said, recommending a hug and a warm greeting instead. Eberhardt also said other people's food choices shouldn't become a group topic and urged letting each guest decide what and how much goes on the plate, adding, "We don't wanna be micromanagers."

item.title: Advisory issued for Utah's mountains after Wasatch Front receives first snow of season
item.description:
Utah's latest storm brought the Wasatch Front its first valley snow of the season and piled 19 inches on Alta and 18 on Snowbird, keeping both on track to open next week. Salt Lake City officially recorded 0.7 inches Tuesday, 40 days earlier in the calendar than its first measurable snow last year, when the capital collected just 3.7 inches all season, its lowest total since record-keeping began in 1874; KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson said "considering last year, we're happy to see this". The National Weather Service has posted winter weather advisories for northern and southern mountain ranges and Wasatch Back towns ahead of a second system expected Thursday into Saturday, with valley rain possibly turning to snow along the Wasatch Front by Friday afternoon.

item.title: Dash camera footage shows Summit County deputies using PIT maneuver in chase
item.description:
A court ordered an arrest warrant Monday for Derek Trevor Holland, 33, after Adult Probation and Parole determined he had broken his probation terms; newly obtained dash camera footage shows a Summit County deputy using a PIT maneuver to end his flight in a stolen car. According to a police affidavit, the Dec. 9, 2025, pursuit on state Route 224 started with a stop over an unlit license plate and topped 100 mph, and the car turned out to have been stolen from Salt Lake City. Holland pleaded guilty to a reduced attempted theft/receiving charge and got a suspended prison term with three years' probation, but has since contested part of the restitution, arguing he admitted only to possessing the car.

item.title: Takeaways from Mullin's testimony on cyber outages, the Texas-LSU flight and immigration
item.description:
Testifying Wednesday before the House Homeland Security Committee, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and intelligence director Jay Clayton insisted that the past week's outages at Microsoft, the FAA, banks and an NSA network were unrelated and not a cyberattack, with Mullin saying he was "98% confident" adversaries weren't involved. Mullin also defended flying to the LSU-Texas game on Saturday while travelers were still stranded by the ground stop, saying the trip had been planned for weeks, that he paid for it, and that canceling with the airspace open might have signaled distrust. On immigration, he said every ICE officer now serving has passed a full background check and anyone lacking one or the full 13 weeks of training is on leave, and when Rep. LaMonica McIver accused him of killing people, he dismissed it as "your opinion".

item.title: University of Utah bringing continuing education program to Asia campus
item.description:
The University of Utah's continuing education program, which dates to 1906 and serves more than 30,000 learners a year, launched Nov. 5 at the U.'s Asia Campus in Incheon, South Korea, the university's first overseas campus, opened in 2013. Ava Choi, who directs continuing education at the Asia Campus, said the courses won't simply be imported from Utah but were designed jointly around South Korean workforce needs, local interests and growing industries, and a university release said the offerings are meant for learners whether or not they are seeking a degree. Randy McCrillis, the U.'s vice provost for continuing education, said the expansion advances the U.'s international mission of "making the university's expertise available to people wherever they are."

item.title: Deportations are up and arrests of Utah immigrants are also on the rise, data shows
item.description:
ICE arrests ending in detention in Utah totaled 7,545 from January 2025 through early August, according to Deportation Data Project figures, with the monthly average climbing from around 285 in the first half of 2025 to 480 from January through July 2026, compared with about 118 a month in 2024. Detainees without criminal convictions grew from 29.2% of Utah detentions in March 2025 to 54.9% last July, while arrests through 287(g) agreements with local law enforcement stayed a small, relatively steady slice after early jumps: 294 since July 2025, most of them in Weber and Washington counties. The data arrives as DHS reports a record 483,200 removals nationwide in fiscal 2026; within Utah, West Valley City led with 1,094 arrests, just ahead of Salt Lake City's 1,025.

item.title: Trump plans separate talks with Putin alongside their 3-way meeting with Xi in China
item.description:
President Donald Trump plans a one-on-one meeting with Vladimir Putin in China on Thursday, on top of a scheduled three-way session with Xi Jinping, a U.S. official told the AP, in what would be their first talks since last year's Alaska meeting failed to yield a Ukraine deal. Trump said he wants to discuss nuclear arms limits and ending the war, saying that "it's very close to getting it done," although his aides had said beforehand that Ukraine was off the agenda and analysts expect no major breakthroughs. The trip to the APEC summit in Shenzhen, where Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac, has been shadowed by outages at Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase and an NSA network, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero" evidence they were linked to one another or to rival nations or hackers.

item.title: How Iran is using social media to exploit US vulnerabilities
item.description:
Alongside Iran's low-cost drones, social media has become a growing asymmetrical threat in the U.S. conflict with Iran: this month the Iranian Embassy in South Africa used X to tell two U.S. Navy officers "We will find you," and another post last weekend mocked Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent and Pete Hegseth over their relocation to military installations following reported threats. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has directed Navy and Marine Corps members to make their accounts private and delete posts that reveal military ties or family routines, writing that "Force protection" is everyone's responsibility. Separately, Senators John Curtis and Mark Kelly said the Army reversed a policy, in place since last June, that barred Dugway and Yuma proving grounds from running their own social media accounts, which the senators had warned would undermine public safety communications.

item.title: 312 pounds of meth seized in UHP drug bust
item.description:
Charles Terry, 63, of Chicago, faces drug distribution charges in 4th District Court after a Utah Highway Patrol stop in Millard County that is believed to rank among the largest drug busts in recent state history. According to a booking affidavit, a trooper pulled over Terry's Jeep Cherokee on I-15 on Oct. 28 over window tint, grew suspicious of three large suitcases for what the driver described as a few days of gambling and shopping in Las Vegas, and after a K-9 alerted found 312 pounds of meth plus two kilos of cocaine/fentanyl in vacuum-sealed packaging. The affidavit also cites "an extensive criminal history" going back to 1983, with past charges that include murder and a prior federal drug case, though details on the murder case weren't immediately available.

item.title: Utah receives $11M from Department of Energy for grid infrastructure projects
item.description:
The U.S. Department of Energy awarded Utah $11 million for its Grid Resilience grant program, part of $967 million handed out nationwide and a follow-up to an $18 million award in 2024 that paid for 11 projects stretching from Box Elder to Washington counties. Utilities, including municipalities and co-ops, can apply starting in 2027, with the required match tied to each utility's annual electricity sales. Emy Lesofski, director of the Utah Office of Energy Development, said producing affordable power is "only half the equation" because the state must also deliver it, while Senate President J. Stuart Adams said the money will help utilities pay for "critical upgrades".

item.title: Kilby Block Party completes its 2027 lineup with a pair of Best New Artist nominees
item.description:
Grammy Best New Artist nominees Remi Wolf and Angine de Poitrine lead the final round of acts added Wednesday to Kilby Block Party, set for May 14-16, 2027, at the Utah State Fairpark, where Deftones, The Strokes and Jungle were already announced as headliners. The Canadian experimental duo Angine de Poitrine, which went viral this year after a KEXP performance, plays May 14, and Wolf, who appeared on American Idol as a teenager in 2014 and whose album Big Ideas made NPR's and Exclaim's best-of-2024 lists, plays May 15; many of the additions had already surfaced on a leaked lineup poster. A Y2 Analytics study for S&S Presents estimated this year's festival drew more than 34,000 attendees, added $33.5 million to Utah's GDP and generated $3.3 million in state and local taxes.

item.title: Intermountain Health celebrates new LDS Hospital downtown, but when will construction begin?
item.description:
Intermountain Health held a ceremonial shovel-turn Tuesday for a new LDS Hospital on the old Sears site near 754 S. State, which will replace the Avenues hospital, but the project still awaits a design review by the city's planning commission, which has yet to schedule a vote. After commissioners raised concerns at a rocky meeting last month, architects made the outpatient pharmacy more accessible, let the public reach a coffee shop and bistro from the street without passing hospital security, and added a "functional greenhouse"; Intermountain is also reviewing exterior materials. LDS Hospital President Heather Wall hopes for a vote in the coming weeks so construction can get underway by the start of 2027, and Councilman Chris Wharton, born at the original hospital, called the downtown site "more accessible" for a growing city.

item.title: Teen organ donor to be honored on 2027 Rose Parade float
item.description:
Morgan White, a 16-year-old Kaysville high school junior whose organs saved four lives after she suffered cardiac arrest in 2024 from CPVT, a rare genetic heart condition, will be pictured in a floragraph portrait on the OneLegacy Donate Life float at the 2027 Rose Parade. Her mother, DaLene White, said she had "no hesitation at all" about donating, and after a DonorConnect Foundation nomination she helped finish the portrait Tuesday by filling in its eyebrows with ground seed. As the float travels the route on New Year's Day, White said, her thoughts will be on the last words Morgan wrote in her journal, about having "100% control to give love to others".

item.title: Season's first major snowfall turns Wasatch into winter playground
item.description:
A family that moved to Utah from South Africa went sledding in the mountains to see snow for the first time, as the season's first major storm turned the Wasatch high country white and sent skiers hiking uphill for early runs before resorts are fully open. One skier called the early snow great compared with last year, and Reef Heikkila predicted "it will be a good season" if it keeps up. More snow is in the forecast for this week as the holidays approach.

item.title: Paramedic mother responds to accident that claimed her son's life in central Utah
item.description:
Sevier County paramedic Tricia Mumford was among the crews answering a Monday evening call in Sigurd and, according to Sheriff Nathan Curtis, realized only after the patient was freed that it was her 28-year-old son, Logan Mumford, pinned when a car slipped off a scissor jack as he helped a woman from his ward replace an alternator. A neighbor who had gone across the street for a floor jack and better lighting could not pull him out, and deputies used that jack to free him before he was flown with severe head injuries to Utah Valley Medical Center; he later died. Fellow paramedic Tyla Northrup, a friend of Tricia Mumford's, said "Nobody can fathom working on their own son," and called Logan Mumford a person who was always ready to help anyone.

item.title: Salt Lake City passes 6-month pause on data centers, seeks future adjustments
item.description:
The Salt Lake City Council unanimously approved a pause of up to six months on new data centers Tuesday, giving the city, and possibly the state, time to write rules before it expires in mid-May. The measure appears to respond to a little-detailed data center proposed in the Northpoint neighborhood, where Florida-based Qlevr LLC sought an air quality permit listing diesel-fired emergency generators, and Councilwoman Victoria Petro, who represents the area, called the project "a thorn in my side". Mayor Erin Mendenhall called it a "healthy pause", saying the city's zoning never contemplated data centers at the scale now being proposed, and the vote follows a Salt Lake County moratorium that covered only unincorporated land.

item.title: Ohio man who sexually abused Utah minor given 45 years in prison
item.description:
A federal judge on Tuesday gave an Ohio man 45 years in prison, followed by probation for life, in a case involving a young Utah girl. Wade S. Christofferson, 73, pleaded guilty in July to a coercion and enticement count; prosecutors say he spent about six months mailing the child sexually coded letters, and that he admitted abusing her during past Utah visits after her father confronted him over inappropriate behavior seen on a FaceTime call. Dominick S. Gerace II, the top federal prosecutor for Ohio's southern district, said the evidence showed "a longstanding sexual interest in children that spanned decades".

item.description:
Democrats will hold 56 of 100 Senate seats when the new Congress starts in January after Mary Peltola unseated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, the party's ninth pickup and its best midterm showing in the chamber since 1958. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," and the party also retook the House, gaining 42 seats as of Tuesday. The Senate has usually been more insulated than the House from midterm swings against the party in power, though second-term midterms are typically rougher.

item.title: Apple joins a parade of technology hiccups in recent days
item.description:
Apple said an internal update caused outages Tuesday that fully knocked out Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare and disrupted iCloud sign-ins, though many systems were back up by the time it issued a statement. The trouble capped a run of breakdowns that included a United Airlines system outage of more than 90 minutes that delayed departures Monday, a JPMorgan Chase technical issue the same day that rippled into other major banks and Zelle, last week's global Microsoft outage hitting Outlook, Teams and Copilot, and the FAA network malfunction behind a nationwide ground stop. Marriott also appeared to have reservation and check-in problems, according to Reddit users, and Downdetector showed an outage there, while United said it saw no sign of a cybersecurity link and Chase and Microsoft both said a cyberattack was not behind their problems.

item.description:
On Tuesday, Intermountain Health held a groundbreaking for a new LDS Hospital on the roughly eight-acre former Sears site at 745 S. State Street, planning a 10-story hospital of more than 521,000 square feet plus a seven-story medical office building; the downtown campus will eventually replace the hospital's longtime home in the Avenues. The downtown campus is to offer emergency, trauma and intensive care, cancer, heart, surgical, and women's and newborn services, a Level II NICU and a public plaza, and Intermountain estimates it will support about 2,000 jobs and more than $1.1 billion a year in local economic impact. The Avenues hospital, open since 1905, will keep running in the meantime with its future still undecided, while LDS Hospital President Heather Wall described the move as "bringing that excellence forward".

item.title: Millburn defeats Lee in Davis County Commission race; Lee backer calls for probe

Unaffiliated former commissioner Brett Millburn beat Republican Susan Lee for a Davis County Commission seat by 55,200 votes to 54,788 in results certified Tuesday, but Lee's campaign manager, Jason Sanders, has asked state and county officials to investigate whether Millburn broke Utah's electioneering law. Sanders points to Millburn's Oct. 20 remarks about his candidacy during public comment at Fruit Heights and Woods Cross council meetings, held in buildings with ballot drop boxes during the mail-in voting period, and said the effort isn't aimed at reversing the result. Millburn's attorney, David Irvine, said election law attorneys read the statute as covering campaigning near polling places or drop boxes on Election Day and called the complaint "the last stand of a desperate and disappointed candidate."

item.title: Utah's crackdown on online betting expands with lawsuit against casino site

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Division of Consumer Protection have sued the companies behind Stake, the world's biggest online casino, alleging that its sweepstakes-style model, in which users buy a virtual currency that converts back to cash one-to-one, is illegal gambling under Utah law. The 3rd District Court complaint, the state's third against a betting platform in the past month, says Stake blocks residents of 25 states but not Utah and courts young audiences with influencers and cartoon-themed slots, and it seeks restitution and penalties "well in excess" of $300,000 each. item.title: Unsheltered Utah expands winter shelter program to serve more neighbors in need
item.description:
Rather than opening only on Code Blue nights, when overnight lows are expected to hit 18 degrees or colder, Unsheltered Utah will run overnight shelter on a regular schedule this winter, Mondays and Thursdays, in partnership with First United Methodist Church and St. Mark's Cathedral. Executive director Merinda Cutler said last year's mild winter meant the group opened just 14 of the 30 nights it was prepared for, and that the church's fellowship hall takes in 73 adults, pets included, with cots, a hot meal and survival supplies. The nonprofit is looking for overnight volunteers and donations, including for a hotel program that, Cutler said, gives families a few nights' stay because the shelter isn't safe for them.

Security Council, the Board of Peace overseeing the U.S.-brokered Gaza ceasefire warned the deal could collapse, citing continued Israeli strikes, Hamas military activity and Israel's failure so far to let the board's interim technocratic administration start work in the territory. Rebuilding, Hamas' disarmament and an Israeli pullout all hinge on an international stabilization force whose deployment has been held up as a result, the report says, and it urges the Security Council to lean on both sides to end the delays. item.title: 'Keep Utah Monumental' campaign launches after cuts to Bears Ears, Grand Staircase-Escalante
item.description:
The Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance on Tuesday launched a Keep Utah Monumental campaign of billboards, digital ads and community organizing aimed at holding Gov. Spencer Cox and Utah's congressional delegation accountable for President Donald Trump's July order cutting Bears Ears to about 121,000 acres and Grand Staircase-Escalante to about 182,000. Cox has said the cuts leave other protections in place while making the monuments "more manageable," but a Deseret News-Hinckley Institute of Politics poll found 56% of Utahns oppose the reductions and 29% support them. Executive director Scott Braden said the midterms show Utah is "changing and changing fast" and that, come January, the delegation will include a member committed to restoring the monuments; that member is Ben McAdams, winner of the race for the 1st Congressional District.
